subject: The first known US wrongful arrest by facial recognition - Robert Julian-Borchak Williams, arrested by Detroit police in 2020 on a false algorithmic face match, and the ACLU case plus 2024 settlement that followed.
central_question: Can a face-recognition algorithm flag YOU as a criminal - and get you arrested for something you did not do?
viewer_promise: By the end, the viewer understands how a grainy store camera plus face-matching software led police to arrest an innocent man in his own driveway in front of his wife and daughters, why the software misidentifies some faces far more often, and what the 2024 settlement changed about when police may act on a face match.
surprise: Robert Williams was arrested for a watch-store theft he had nothing to do with. The evidence was a face-recognition match run on a blurry surveillance still - the software picked him, the detectives ran with it, and he spent about 30 hours in jail before anyone noticed he looked nothing like the actual thief. It was the first such wrongful arrest to come to light in the US; it was not the last.
stakes: Whether an automated guess about your face is enough to put you in handcuffs; why the technology is measurably less accurate on some faces than others; and what a citizen can actually do when an algorithm names them.
target_audience: English-speaking US general audience; anyone with a face and a phone; maximally relatable and largely unknown to the public - a real, sympathetic person versus an invisible algorithm.
demand_evidence: Facial recognition wrongful arrest is a live, growing news topic (multiple documented cases since 2020) with strong search and social interest.

Channel analytics show the winning vein is second-person can-the-police-do-X-to-YOU surveillance/phone stories (Riley phone search, Carpenter phone tracking); a face-recognition wrongful arrest is that exact vein applied to YOUR face.
Obscure specific victim plus a shocking, relatable premise (an algorithm got the wrong man) equals high curiosity gap, low direct competition.
competition: Tech and news outlets covered the Williams case in bursts; few tell the full human story end to end - the driveway arrest, the 30 hours, the bias data, and the settlement - sourced and neutral.
differentiation: A true-story-forward, obscure-but-universal surveillance episode: one sympathetic father versus a face-matching algorithm, a clean second-person hook (this could be your face), the documented racial-accuracy gap, and the 2024 settlement payoff - sourced to the ACLU record and contemporaneous reporting. Sits in the proven phone/surveillance vein (Riley/Carpenter).
research_feasibility: High: ACLU of Michigan case materials (Williams v. City of Detroit), the 2024 settlement announcement, contemporaneous reporting (NYT/Washington Post 2020), NIST FRVT plus MIT Gender Shades studies on demographic accuracy gaps, and Detroit PD revised facial-recognition policy are public.
visual_feasibility: High: a suburban driveway arrest reconstruction (anonymous figures), a grainy store-camera still vs a face-match grid, an accuracy/bias bar chart, a booking/holding-cell reconstruction, a family home, a timeline (2018 theft to 2020 arrest to 2024 settlement). No real-person likeness (invariant 11); Williams described accurately per the public record.
risk_notes: Real, named private individual (Robert Julian-Borchak Williams) as a sympathetic protagonist: describe strictly and accurately per the public record and the ACLU case; NO real-person likeness in AI visuals (invariant 11).
Race is central to the accuracy-gap story: present the measured NIST/MIT findings factually and neutrally, without inflammatory framing.
Detroit PD and the software vendor described factually per the record; systemic-technology story, not an accusation against named officers.
Facial-recognition law/policy varies by jurisdiction and is evolving; flag as changing, not a single nationwide rule.
Generated visuals are illustration/reconstruction, never presented as authentic footage.
kill_conditions: Cannot source the wrongful arrest, the false face-match basis, and the 2024 settlement to the ACLU record plus one independent authoritative report.
